title: Finding and reviewing delegated agency discretion
shortTitle: Finding and reviewing delegated agency discretion
summary: Delegated discretion is a range of choices that Congress has authorized an agency to make within statutory boundaries.
notes:
The reviewing court determines the legal boundaries of that range. Loper Bright identifies express delegations to define terms, authority to fill details, and flexible standards such as reasonable or appropriate as examples of statutes that can authorize agency choices. The agency must then choose within the range and give the reasoned explanation required by the APA. The court’s independent interpretation of the boundary coexists with deferential review of the agency’s permitted policy judgment. (Printed 945–946, 950.)

This distinction explains both continuity and change after Chevron. The earlier doctrine presumed delegation from unresolved ambiguity more broadly. Loper Bright requires an independent legal finding that the statute actually assigns discretion. The casebook’s proposed framework suggests that clear statutory answers and genuine open-ended policy grants may produce continuity, while former step-two choices between alternative legal meanings change decisionmaker. The authors present that as an analytical framework, not as a holding quantifying how many cases will change. (Printed 963–964.)

West Virginia adds the requirement of clear authorization for the extraordinary power at issue there. Kisor separately addresses interpretations of agency regulations and requires a contextual inquiry into whether deference is justified. Kavanaugh’s Kisor concurrence describes a reasonable policy choice within an open-ended regulation as a State Farm issue. These doctrines interact, but a classification as agency discretion does not itself establish the scope of the statute, the validity of a regulation, or the adequacy of the reasons given. (Printed 972–975, 999–1000.)
